Where is Hinds County and how is it laid out?

Hinds County sits in central Mississippi and is the state's most populous county, with 227,742 residents at the 2020 census. It covers 877 square miles, of which 870 are land, and it has two county seats: Jackson and Raymond.

That two-seat arrangement shapes almost every property tax errand. The county is split into a First Judicial District (Jackson) and a Second Judicial District (Raymond), and the tax collector, tax assessor and chancery clerk each keep an office in both places.

The cities are Byram, Clinton, Jackson and Raymond. The towns are Bolton, Edwards, Learned, Terry and Utica, and unincorporated places such as Brownsville, Cayuga, Cynthia, Midway, Oakley and Pocahontas fill in the rural parts. Part of Jackson lies in Madison and Rankin counties, so check which county bills a given parcel.

Interstates 20, 55 and 220 cross the county, along with US 49, US 51 and US 80, and a stretch of the Natchez Trace Parkway runs through it. Public-use airports are Hawkins Field in Jackson and John Bell Williams Airport in Raymond.

Which Hinds County offices handle property tax?

Three elected offices share the work: the tax assessor values property, the tax collector sends bills and takes payment, and the chancery clerk records deeds, runs the appeal hearing process through the Board of Supervisors, and collects delinquent taxes. Each has a Jackson and a Raymond location, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday except legal holidays.

OfficeJackson (First District)Raymond (Second District)
Tax Collector316 S. President St., 601-968-6587127 W. Main St., 601-857-5574
Tax AssessorMail: P.O. Box 22908, 601-968-6616Mail: P.O. Box 549, 601-857-8787
Chancery Clerk316 S. President St., 601-968-6508Main St. Annex Building, 601-857-8055

The numbers above come from the county's own office pages and can change, so call before you drive.

You can read each office's page on the county site: Tax Collector, Tax Assessor and Chancery Clerk.

How does the Hinds County assessor value a house?

The assessor lists every taxable parcel, estimates its value, applies the state assessment ratio and certifies a roll to the Board of Supervisors. The office says its territory runs from Learned, with about 100 parcels, up to the City of Jackson, with more than 70,000, and totals over 106,000 parcels.

Under the state's classes, a single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I and is assessed at 10 percent of true value. Other real estate, such as a rental house, is Class II at 15 percent. The Mississippi Department of Revenue explains that taxes equal true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate.

Hinds County says it reviews 25 percent of taxable property each year, so every parcel is looked at at least once every four years. For most houses that means a drive-by comparison against the drawings and field sheet in the office. The assessor only contacts an owner if what the appraiser sees differs from the file. The state adds that interior inspections of homes are not required.

The office also runs sales ratio studies, comparing appraised values with actual sale prices, and the State Tax Commission does its own.

  • Ownership is set as of January 1 using deeds filed with the chancery clerk.
  • The assessment roll goes to the Board of Supervisors on the first Monday in July.
  • The office's past policy has been to notify owners when a new appraisal rises $2,000 or more over the prior year.

What dates matter on a Hinds County tax bill?

Taxes are due on or before February 1 for property assessed the previous year, and if February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday, payment is accepted the next Monday without penalty. The chancery clerk's office says statements are mailed from the tax collector each December and that current taxes may be paid in three installments.

DateWhat happens
January 1Owner of record is fixed for the assessment year
January 1 to April 1Homestead exemption applications accepted
First Monday in JulyAssessment roll presented to the Board of Supervisors
First Monday in AugustNormal deadline to file an assessment appeal
November to DecemberTax bills issued
February 1Taxes due without interest
Last Monday in AugustUnpaid taxes go to tax sale

After February 1, state law adds interest of one-half of one percent per month, or fraction of a month, on unpaid tax. The governor can extend that date by proclamation for unusual conditions, for up to 60 days at a time.

How do I appeal a Hinds County assessment?

You ask the county Board of Supervisors for a hearing, and the Chancery Clerk is the contact for that request. The state says an appeal normally has to be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax comes due.

Start earlier, though. The Hinds assessor says its office will review values with an owner at any time of year, and its page describes the formal appeal as the next step under Mississippi Code 27-35-89. For business personal property, the office posts values after the first Monday in July, offers review through July 31, and says a formal protest must reach the chancery clerk by 9:00 a.m. on the first Monday in August.

Bring evidence about value. Lafayette County's appeal guide says boards weigh the fairness and accuracy of the value and that a recent appraisal of your own house is the best exhibit. Hinds has not published matching guidance we could confirm, but the same logic applies.

If an appraisal has the wrong square footage, the state says you may sometimes get a refund for prior years through the chancery clerk.

What happens if Hinds County taxes go unpaid?

The house goes to the county tax sale on the last Monday in August, and if nobody bids, it is struck off to the state. The chancery clerk collects delinquent taxes, and once a year is delinquent the clerk says the older years must be cleared before the current year can be paid.

The clerk's page lists some firm rules for delinquent payments: no installments, and payment by cash or money order only, with no personal checks. The owner has two years from the sale date to redeem. If the two years pass, the property either matures to the state or the buyer receives a tax deed, which the clerk's own page describes as meaning you no longer own the property.

The state also publishes a Secretary of State line, 1-866-835-2637, for property that was sold to the state. Hinds posts delinquent and tax sale lists on its county site.

  • Redemption means paying the delinquent taxes plus statutory damages and interest, as Mississippi courts have described it.
  • An owner who sells before the sale date can clear the taxes from the sale proceeds.
  • An owner who waits until after the sale can still redeem, but only through the chancery clerk.

Selling a Hinds County house when property tax is still owed

You can sell a house with unpaid taxes, because taxes are cleared through the title and closing process. A title search turns up any back taxes, mortgages or other liens, and the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

The chancery clerk's guidance for buyers is useful for sellers too. A title search should be done before any money changes hands, and any attorney or title company can do it. The clerk's office itself may not search the records or prepare a deed. A deed must carry the seller's notarized signature, a legal description with indexing instructions, and the names, addresses and phone numbers of the sellers, buyers and preparer.

Timing matters if the house is occupied by an owner. The clerk notes that a buyer who occupies the home before January 1 can apply for homestead exemption from January 1 to April 1, which lowers that year's tax. A cash sale to an investor generally does not change the sequence, because the recording and tax steps are the same. It mainly removes the wait for a buyer's lender.

Sellers in Hinds County often arrive with older homes, inherited houses or rentals. Probate and heirship questions go to the chancery court, which hears probate and land matters, and the clerk's office files those papers. If the owner has died, clearing title may need to happen before a deed can be signed.

What should Hinds County sellers know about the local market around them?

Hinds County's economy leans on government, health care and education centered in Jackson. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Hinds County employment of 109,600 in December 2024, the highest of any Mississippi county. The University of Mississippi Medical Center, based in Jackson, says it has more than 10,000 full- and part-time employees.

Public schools are served by three districts: Jackson Public School District, Clinton Public School District and Hinds County School District. State-run schools for the blind and the deaf are also in the county. Colleges include Jackson State University, Millsaps College, Belhaven University, Mississippi College in Clinton and Hinds Community College in Raymond.

Population has been falling. The Census Bureau counted 250,998 people in 1980 and 227,742 in 2020, and estimates 211,888 for 2025. For a seller, that trend can mean fewer buyers per listing, and a clean tax record removes one obstacle to closing.

Frequently asked questions

When are Hinds County property taxes due?

Taxes are due on or before February 1 for the previous assessment year. If that date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, you have until the next Monday without penalty or interest. After that, interest of one-half of one percent per month applies.

Where do I pay property tax in Hinds County?

You pay the Hinds County Tax Collector, which has offices at 316 S. President St. in Jackson and 127 W. Main St. in Raymond. The office accepts cash, check or credit card with a 2.25 percent surcharge, and tags paid by personal check are held for 10 working days.

What is the Hinds County assessment ratio for a home?

An owner-occupied single-family home is assessed at 10 percent of true value, and other real property such as a rental is assessed at 15 percent. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined millage rate of the county, city and school district.

What is the deadline to appeal a Hinds County property assessment?

Normally the first Monday in August before the tax is due. You request a hearing with the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk, so start with the assessor well before that date.

Can I sell my Hinds County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the back taxes from your proceeds at closing. If the house has already gone to tax sale, the chancery clerk collects the redemption amount, and the owner has two years from the sale date to redeem.

Where is DeSoto County, Mississippi, and how is it laid out?

DeSoto County sits in the northwest corner of Mississippi, directly south of Shelby County, Tennessee, and its county seat is Hernando. The county covers 497 square miles, of which 476 are land, and it borders Crittenden County, Arkansas, to the west across the Mississippi River, plus Tunica, Tate and Marshall counties.

Most people live in four cities: Hernando, Horn Lake, Olive Branch and Southaven. The county also has one town, Walls, several census-designated places such as Lake View, Lynchburg and Pleasant Hill, and unincorporated communities like Lake Cormorant, Nesbit and Cockrum. Where a house sits decides which city or school levy shows up on the bill, so the first step for any seller is to look at the parcel's tax district.

How did DeSoto County grow into a Memphis suburb?

The county was organized in 1836 and farmed cotton first, then dairy and soybeans, before subdivisions replaced the fields. According to a county history on the county website, soybean acreage passed cotton by 1970, and by 1999 only three dairies were left.

The same history marks the turning points that built the housing stock you see today:

  • Homes in the Southaven community went on sale in 1958, and the city was incorporated on March 25, 1980.
  • Interstate 55 opened through Hernando in 1964.
  • New one-family homes ran above 1,000 a year in the early 1970s.
  • The county's population was 67,910 in 1990, according to the 1990 census, and the Wikipedia table of census counts shows 107,199 in 2000 and 161,252 in 2010.

For a seller this means DeSoto County houses span several building eras. A 1970s ranch in Horn Lake and a 2010s two-story in Olive Branch will face very different repair lists, even though both are billed by the same collector.

What do roads and schools mean for a DeSoto County house?

Four routes carry most traffic: Interstate 55, Interstate 69, Interstate 269, plus U.S. 51 and U.S. 61. The county has no fixed-route transit of its own. Memphis Area Transit Authority, Amtrak, Greyhound and other carriers serve nearby Memphis instead, so most households depend on a car.

Public education is run by one district, the DeSoto County School District, which covers the whole county and is the largest in the state. That keeps school boundaries simple compared with counties that split among several districts, although attendance zones still differ by address.

Who assesses and who collects property tax in DeSoto County?

The Tax Assessor values the property and the Tax Collector bills and collects it. Both offices are in Hernando. The county lists the Tax Collector at 365 Losher Street, Suite 110, Hernando, phone 662-469-8030, with a second office on BJ Chain Drive in Olive Branch. A city notice from Hernando places the Tax Assessor at 365 Losher Street, Suite 100, and the county homestead page gives the assessor's phone as 662-469-8029.

Under state law the assessor must revalue real property at least once every four years, and taxable personal property every year. Interior inspections of homes are not required, according to the Mississippi Department of Revenue. Voters do not set your rate directly. The county, the city and the school district each decide what they need, and local officials turn that into a millage rate.

Class IIOther real property, such as rentals and land15%

Class VMotor vehicles30%

The state formula is true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. A rental house in DeSoto County lands in Class II, so it is assessed at a higher share of value than an owner-occupied home, before millage is applied.

When are DeSoto County property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?

Mississippi property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1, bills go out in November and December, and the tax is due by February 1. If February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the Department of Revenue says payment is accepted the following Monday without penalty or interest. DeSoto County's own audited financial statements say taxes on real and personal property are due on or before February 1 of the following year.

If real estate taxes stay unpaid, the parcel can go to the county tax sale. The state says some counties hold that sale on the first Monday in April and others on the last Monday in August, so confirm the date with the collector.

  • A buyer who purchases at a tax sale does not take clear title right away. The owner can redeem within two years of the sale, according to Mississippi Supreme Court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3.
  • If nobody buys the parcel at the sale, it goes to the State of Mississippi and is handled by the Secretary of State, phone 1-866-835-2637.
  • Delinquent taxes are a lien problem for a sale. A title company will want them paid at closing.

How do I appeal a DeSoto County assessment?

You ask for a hearing before the county Board of Supervisors, and the Chancery Clerk is the contact for the process. The Department of Revenue says an appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax is due.

Before filing, call the assessor's office with comparable sales or repair estimates in hand. If your home needs a new roof or has foundation damage, photographs and contractor quotes carry more weight than an opinion. The board reviews valuations, hears objections and adopts the rolls, which is why the August date matters.

Does homestead exemption matter when you sell a DeSoto County house?

Yes, because it lowers the bill the buyer inherits and it does not carry over automatically after a sale. Applications are filed with the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and the state says you do not have to reapply each year unless something changes, such as ownership or marital status.

People 65 or older, and people who are totally disabled and otherwise eligible, are exempt from taxes on the first $75,000 of true value, according to the Department of Revenue. Homestead is not allowed if the owner or spouse is out of compliance with state income tax laws or has a vehicle tagged outside the county of the home. A buyer who plans to live in the house should file in their first year, since missing April 1 means waiting for the next assessment year.

What do sellers in DeSoto County usually face?

Sellers here often deal with a mix of timing, repairs and carrying costs. A few patterns come up again and again:

  • Check that the owner name, mailing address and homestead status on the roll are current, since a bill sent to the wrong address is still due.
  • Inherited homes anywhere in the county can carry unpaid taxes or unrecorded paperwork that must be cleared before closing.
  • Rentals in Class II carry a higher assessment ratio, which matters to an investor selling a tenant-occupied house.
  • Newer subdivisions can sit in a city levy, while a house outside city limits does not, so two similar homes can have different bills.

A cash sale can shorten that list because the buyer purchases as-is and closes on a date you choose. You still need a clean title, a payoff for any mortgage and the current tax paid or settled on the closing statement. We do not promise a price, and you can compare any offer against a listing before deciding.

How do I check what I owe before selling?

Start with the county's online tax search, which lists real and personal property by name, parcel or address and shows amounts due. Then confirm with the collector by phone, since tax-sale and prior-year balances can appear separately.

  1. Find the parcel number on your deed or the assessor's lookup.
  2. Check the current and prior-year balances with the Tax Collector in Hernando or Olive Branch.
  3. Ask the Chancery Clerk whether any past sale exists on the parcel.
  4. Give your title company the figures so they can settle taxes at closing.

Where do I pay property tax in DeSoto County?

You pay the DeSoto County Tax Collector. The county lists an office at 365 Losher Street, Suite 110, Hernando, phone 662-469-8030, and another in Olive Branch. Call before you go, since hours and payment methods can change.

Yes. Unpaid taxes are paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, and the title company will ask for a payoff figure. If the parcel already went to a tax sale, the redemption amount also has to be settled, and Mississippi allows two years from the sale to redeem.

Does DeSoto County have one school district?

Lowndes County overview

Columbus is the seat and the only city of Lowndes County, which hugs the Alabama line on Mississippi's eastern side. The count was 58,879 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 57,346, a decline of 2.6 percent. Housing demand is steady rather than booming, tied to manufacturing, Columbus Air Force Base and the Mississippi University for Women.

Two public school systems serve the county, the Columbus Municipal School District and the Lowndes County School District, and the tax bill depends partly on which one covers your address. Each taxing body picks its own levy, and the sum becomes your millage rate. Towns such as Caledonia, Artesia and Crawford, plus rural areas to the west, make up the rest of the market for sellers.

The Lowndes County Tax Office

The Tax Office is at 1121 Main Street in Columbus, MS 39701. Call 662-329-5700 to reach the tax collector, or 662-329-3940 for the assessor's mapping line. The county's own site is lowndescountyms.com. Search results for a similarly named county in another state can show a different due date, so stay on that address.

TaskWhere to do it

A parcel lookup is the best first step before you talk to any buyer: the record shows the assessed value, the ratio applied and whether any year is open. The Tax Office page has the current office hours, so look there or call before you drive in.

When Lowndes County property taxes are due

The bill covers the prior year's assessment and must be paid on or before February 1. Should that day be a weekend or legal holiday, Monday becomes the last penalty-free day. Ownership is fixed on January 1, and the statement shows up in the mail around November or December.

  • January 1 to April 1: window to apply for homestead exemption.
  • First Monday in August: usual deadline to appeal with the Board of Supervisors.
  • February 1: payment due.
  • Past February 1: one-half of one percent interest each month.

If you are listing in the fall, ask the buyer's side early who is taking the bill that arrives in November or December. The usual approach is to split the bill by closing date, and the split belongs in writing in the contract or on the settlement statement.

Appealing your assessment

If the value looks wrong, ask the Chancery Clerk to put you on the Board of Supervisors' hearing list. Plan to do it by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

Real property in Mississippi has to be revalued at least once every four years, so your number can move when your parcel comes up. Interior inspections of houses are not required, and the assessor values every structure on a parcel, outbuildings included. If your house was recorded at the wrong size, a refund for earlier years may be possible through the Chancery Clerk.

Before you file, ask the assessor's staff to walk you through the value on the roll. Bring photos, any recent appraisal and recent sales of similar houses.

Homestead exemption

Homestead exemption covers the house you live in. Take the application to the assessor in the county where the house stands before April 1, and not earlier than January 1. It carries over from year to year, but you should file again if your marital status or ownership changes.

An owner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled, and who meets the other tests can shield the first $75,000 of true value. Proof of disability may include a VA release form, a Social Security benefit report or letters from two physicians. Falling behind on state income tax filings, for you or a spouse, can cost you eligibility, and so can registering a vehicle in a different county.

An inherited house that no one lives in gets no homestead, so expect the 15 percent ratio on it rather than 10.

What happens to unpaid taxes?

Land with unpaid taxes is offered at the county tax sale, and the former owner keeps a two-year right to buy it back. A redeeming owner pays the delinquent taxes, the buyer's money comes back with monthly interest, and if two years pass with no redemption the buyer can get a tax deed from the chancery clerk. The county has run its sale online through GovEase.

The statutes put these auctions on either the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August. Which one applies this year is a question for the Tax Office. For land already sold to the state, call the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637.

If you are behind, selling ahead of the auction date is the easy way out, because the title company settles the taxes from what you receive. If the auction has already happened, the redemption amount is the figure to get, and the Chancery Clerk or the Tax Office can supply it. Keep the paperwork from any payment, because a buyer's title company will ask to see it.

Selling a Lowndes County house

A sale here follows the usual Mississippi steps: title search, a prepared deed, payment of taxes and liens at closing, and recording with the chancery clerk.

  1. Pull the parcel on the Property Link search and read the assessed value and tax status.
  2. Get a payoff number from the Tax Office for each year that is past due.
  3. Confirm whether homestead is on file. It is the difference between a 10 percent ratio on a home you occupy and 15 percent on everything else.
  4. For an inherited house, the chancery court handles probate and the clerk files the papers.
  5. Pick an attorney or title company early so the deed and closing are ready.

Owners in Columbus, Caledonia, New Hope and the rural west sometimes sell as-is because of repairs, a move for work or an estate. A cash buyer closes without a bank appraisal or a lender's repair list. Cash Home Buyers reviews every Lowndes County house on its own facts, and we name no price or closing date until we have seen the details.

Bring your deed, a recent tax receipt and any mortgage payoff statement to the first conversation with a title company. Those three papers settle most early questions about who holds title, what is owed and which county office has to sign off on the numbers. Heirs should add the probate paperwork, and landlords should add any lease that is still running.

Frequently asked questions

When are Lowndes County, MS property taxes due?

The deadline is February 1. A Saturday, Sunday or holiday deadline rolls to Monday, and any bill paid after that picks up one-half of one percent a month.

Where is the Lowndes County Tax Office?

It is at 1121 Main Street in Columbus, MS 39701, phone 662-329-5700. An online county portal takes real property tax, personal property tax and car tag payments.

What is the Lowndes County appeal deadline?

Usually the first Monday in August. Contact the Chancery Clerk to get a hearing in front of the Board of Supervisors.

How do I confirm I am on the right county website?

Use lowndescountyms.com, the Mississippi county's site. A similarly named site for a county in another state lists a different due date.

Can I sell my Lowndes County house if taxes are overdue?

Yes. The title company pays back taxes from your proceeds at closing. A parcel the county has already auctioned stays redeemable for two years from the auction date.

What makes Harrison County, Mississippi different from other Gulf Coast counties?

Harrison County has two county seats, Gulfport and Biloxi, and the county assessor runs a separate office in each judicial district. It was established on February 5, 1841, from parts of Hancock, Jackson and Perry counties, and it is named for President William Henry Harrison.

The total area as 976 square miles, of which 402 square miles (41%) is water, making it the second-largest county in Mississippi by total area. The Tchoutacabouffa River reaches Biloxi Bay just north of Biloxi, and Gulfport is the state's chief port, with a ship channel to the Gulf of Mexico.

How has storm history shaped Harrison County housing?

Two hurricanes define the county's building history: Camille on August 17, 1969, and Katrina on August 29, 2005, both of which Wikipedia describes as causing catastrophic damage. Hurricane Georges in 1998 also pushed the Tchoutacabouffa River over its banks near Old Highway 67 and Mississippi 15.

For a seller, that history shows up in questions a buyer asks first. Is the lot in a flood zone, was the house rebuilt after a storm, and is the roof recent? Ask your insurer and the county for the facts on your own parcel.

The county also has an older layer of history. The French built Fort Maurepas in 1699, hotels opened along the coast in the 1880s, and Keesler Field arrived in the early to mid 1900s. That mix explains why a Biloxi bungalow, a Long Beach cottage and a newer D'Iberville subdivision can have so little in common.

Who handles property tax in Harrison County?

The Tax Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills it, with offices in both judicial districts. According to the Tax Assessor's page, the office is responsible for more than 100,000 parcels of real and personal property.

  • Assessor, Gulfport: 1801 23rd Avenue, phone 228-865-4043.
  • Assessor, Biloxi: 730 Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd., phone 228-435-8266.
  • Office hours for the assessor are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday.
  • Collector offices: Gulfport (1801 23rd Avenue), Biloxi (730 Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd.) and the Multi-Services Building at 12423 Seaway Road, Gulfport. Phone 228-865-4039 or 228-865-4040, option 3.
  • The collector also runs kiosks at D'Iberville, Long Beach and Pass Christian city halls.

The county also offers an online land roll search and a GIS mapping page through the assessor, which helps you confirm the parcel, owner name and legal description before a sale.

How does Harrison County turn value into a tax bill?

The assessor sets true value, the state's ratio for the class gives the assessed value, and the millage rate does the rest. The county explains that the Tax Assessor is not involved in setting the millage rate, which comes from the taxing agencies: municipalities, schools and the County Board of Supervisors.

True value for Class I and II property is based on current use, regardless of location, under the Mississippi Appraisal Manual language quoted on the county site. That detail matters for a beachfront owner who assumes the water view will drive the assessment.

What is the Harrison County tax calendar?

Statements are mailed December 1, taxes are due by February 1, and interest of one half of one percent per month starts February 2. The Tax Collector's page spells out the rest of the year:

  1. Bills for the 2025 roll began collecting on December 1, 2025, in all three offices.
  2. The collector honors the postmark when figuring monthly interest on mailed payments.
  3. Delinquent real property is published in the newspaper in July, and no partial payments are accepted after that.
  4. The tax sale is held on the last Monday in August, and payment must arrive by 5:00 p.m. the Friday before.
  5. Parcels sold can be redeemed through the Chancery Clerk, normally opening by October 1.
  6. Personal property taxes unpaid on September 30 go to an attorney, adding 20% of the total due.
  7. Mobile home taxes go out January 1 and are due February 1.

The county says it sends the sale list to GovEase and will not pull a parcel once it has been handed over. Only certified funds are accepted to take part in the sale, and the office warns against mailing a check the week before it.

What is the redemption period after a Harrison County tax sale?

The owner has two years from the date of the tax sale to redeem, according to Mississippi Supreme Court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. The Chancery Clerk must notify the owner of the sale and of the right to redeem.

This affects a seller in two ways. First, a house that already went through a sale cannot close until the redemption is settled. Second, the Department of Revenue says land nobody buys goes to the State, and the Secretary of State handles it at 1-866-835-2637.

If you are close to the August deadline, the county suggests paying by phone at 228-865-4040, option 3, rather than relying on the mail.

How do I appeal a Harrison County assessment?

Ask the Board of Supervisors for a hearing, and contact the Chancery Clerk for the process. The Department of Revenue says an appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax is due.

Before you file, call the assessor in Gulfport or Biloxi and bring documents, such as repair bids or a recent appraisal. The state also notes that interior inspections are not required, so an assessor's value for your house may rest on exterior facts. If the record misstates square footage, ask about a correction and a possible refund for earlier years through the Chancery Clerk.

Does homestead exemption matter when selling in Harrison County?

It does, because the buyer's bill depends on whether they claim it. Homestead applications are filed with the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and you need not reapply every year unless something changes.

Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and who otherwise qualify are exempt from tax on the first $75,000 of true value. Military members stationed outside Mississippi can qualify if they claim Mississippi residency and comply with state law, and both spouses must qualify.

What do Harrison County sellers usually face?

A few recurring issues deserve attention before you list or accept a cash offer:

  • An unpaid balance close to the August sale, since the Friday deadline is firm.
  • Damage or repairs left from a storm, which can block a conventional buyer's loan.
  • A mobile home that was moved or destroyed but still appears on the roll. The county says you must tell the Tax Assessor, with proof, to remove it.
  • Inherited houses where taxes lapsed while the family sorted out ownership.

Taxes are due by February 1, with interest of 0.5% per month starting February 2. Statements are mailed December 1. The collector uses the postmark date to figure interest on mailed payments.

It is held on the last Monday in August. Real property taxes must be paid by 5:00 p.m. the Friday before, because the list goes to GovEase and parcels are not pulled once it is handed over.

Where do I pay property taxes in Harrison County?

You can pay at the Gulfport, Biloxi or Multi-Services Building offices, online through the county's payment link, by phone at 228-865-4040 option 3, or at kiosks in D'Iberville, Long Beach and Pass Christian.

Can I redeem a Harrison County parcel after the tax sale?

Yes. Mississippi gives the owner two years from the sale to redeem, according to court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. Redemption runs through the Chancery Clerk, which normally opens it by October 1 after a sale.

How do I appeal my Harrison County assessment?

Request a hearing with the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk. The state says appeals normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax is due.

Jackson County at a glance

Down in Mississippi's southeastern corner, Jackson County borders the Gulf of Mexico about 190 miles from the state capital. It has no connection to the city of Jackson, which is in Hinds County. The county seat is Pascagoula, and the other cities are Gautier, Moss Point and Ocean Springs. Vancleave, Escatawpa, Gulf Park Estates and Latimer are among the unincorporated communities.

The population was 143,252 in 2020 and is estimated at 147,666 for 2025, up from 118,015 in 1980. The county is heavily industrial, with shipbuilding, refinery and manufacturing jobs around Pascagoula, Moss Point and Ocean Springs. Steady employment like that brings buyers who want to live close to work. Storm-exposed and older houses tend to sit longer on the market.

Interstate 10 and US 90 run east and west through the county, and state highways 57, 63 and 609 run north. Much of the county is water or protected land, so a lot of the housing is packed along the coast and the main roads.

Tax assessor and tax collector offices

Jackson County is one of 17 Mississippi counties that keep the tax assessor and the tax collector as separate offices. A sale touches both desks. The assessor owns the value and the exemptions, while the collector owns the bill and the payment.

OfficeWhat it handlesContact
Tax AssessorReal property appraisal, business personal property, homestead exemptionDepartments for Real Property Appraisal, Personal Property (Business) and Homestead
Tax CollectorBills and collects real and personal property tax2915 Canty Street, Pascagoula; mail to Box 998, Pascagoula, MS 39568; 228-769-3074; Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Both offices have pages on the county website: Tax Collector and Tax Assessor. Parts of those pages load slowly, so call before you drive over. Ask the same call whether the collector has a drop box if you would rather not wait in line.

Property tax calendar

Whoever holds title on January 1 is the owner of record for that year's bill. Statements are mailed in November or December, and the payment deadline is February 1. When that date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, Monday is the effective cutoff and no interest is charged. Miss it and Mississippi Code 27-41-9 adds interest of one-half of one percent for every month the bill sits unpaid.

  • January 1: assessment date and ownership date.
  • April 1: deadline for homestead exemption, builder affidavits and business personal property renditions.
  • First Monday in July: the assessment rolls are presented.
  • First Monday in August: the Board of Supervisors starts hearing appeals.
  • February 1: payment due date.

A closing that falls near any of these dates needs a little planning. Decide in the purchase contract who covers the February 1 bill, then ask the title company to show that split on the settlement statement so nobody argues about it later. If you are listing in spring, mention the April 1 homestead deadline to your buyer too, since a missed filing means a full-rate bill.

How hurricanes affect taxes and house sales

Storms are part of this county's property record. Hurricane Camille hit in August 1969 and Hurricane Katrina on August 29, 2005, and both did catastrophic damage along the coast.

State law builds in some relief for payment delays. Under Mississippi Code 27-41-9, the governor may extend the date for charging interest by proclamation when unusual conditions delay payment through no fault of the taxpayer or the collector. The extension can run up to 60 days, with two more extensions possible. The state tax agency has also published guidance on possible relief under section 27-35-143(9), which lets boards of supervisors adjust assessments in certain circumstances. Ask the chancery clerk whether that section applies to your parcel.

Unrepaired roof or water damage lowers a house's value and can block a buyer's financing, because a lender's inspector may refuse to sign off. That is why owners here sometimes sell as-is. If you think storm damage should lower your assessment, the appeal window closes on the first Monday in August.

Why neighbors can pay different amounts

Four public school districts divide the county. The Jackson County School District covers Hurley, Wade, Big Point, Three Rivers, Harleston, Vestry, Latimer and Vancleave, plus St. Martin and a small part of Escatawpa. Pascagoula-Gautier serves Pascagoula and most of Gautier, Moss Point serves Moss Point and most of Escatawpa, and Ocean Springs serves Ocean Springs.

The county, each city and each school district set their own levy, and they add together into one millage rate. A house worth the same money can carry a bigger or smaller bill depending on which side of a district line it sits. Find out your district before quoting a tax figure to a buyer.

What happens to unpaid Jackson County taxes?

Unpaid real estate tax puts the property in line for the county tax auction. The state permits these sales on the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August. The collector's office can tell you which date this county uses.

Losing the sale does not end your claim right away. The former owner has two years counted from the sale date to buy the property back, paying the overdue taxes along with statutory damages and interest, and the chancery clerk is supposed to send notice of that right. Only if the two years run out does the buyer become eligible for a tax deed. For land sold to the state, the Secretary of State can be reached at 1-866-835-2637.

Selling with taxes, liens or storm damage

Owing back taxes does not stop a sale. A title search finds the balance and the closing agent pays it from your proceeds, the same way a lien or a leftover mortgage balance is paid.

  1. Get a written payoff number for any past-due taxes from the collector before you list or say yes to an offer.
  2. Confirm your homestead status. A single-family home you live in is assessed at 10 percent of value rather than 15 percent, and you apply between January 1 and April 1.
  3. Collect insurance and repair records if the house had flood or wind damage.
  4. Have an attorney or title company draw up the deed.
  5. On closing day the payoffs come out of what you are owed, the buyer signs, and the title company sends the new deed for recording.

With no lender in the picture, a cash purchase can close faster on a house that would fail a financing inspection. Cash Home Buyers looks at each Jackson County property individually and does not set a price or a timeline until we have the details.

Frequently asked questions

Is Jackson County, MS the same as Jackson, MS?

No. Jackson County is on the Mississippi Gulf Coast with Pascagoula as its seat, about 190 miles from the city of Jackson, which is in Hinds County. Each place has its own property tax office.

When are property taxes due in Jackson County, Mississippi?

By February 1 each year. A weekend or holiday deadline slides to Monday with no interest. After that, interest builds at one-half of one percent each month.

Where do I pay Jackson County property tax?

Pay the Tax Collector at 2915 Canty Street in Pascagoula, or mail it to Box 998, Pascagoula, MS 39568. The phone is 228-769-3074, and the office is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays.

How do I appeal a Jackson County assessment?

Ask the Chancery Clerk to set a hearing before the Board of Supervisors. File by the first Monday in August, the day hearings begin.

Can I sell a Jackson County, MS house after hurricane damage?

Yes. Buyers who accept the repairs will take a damaged house as-is. Taxes owed come out of the proceeds, and the title company checks for liens first.

Rankin County in brief

Rankin County lies in central Mississippi along the Pearl River, right beside Hinds County and the Jackson area. Brandon is the county seat. Brandon, Florence, Flowood, Pearl, Pelahatchie, Puckett, Richland, Sandhill and Star are the communities the county lists, and Pearl is the largest city. The 2020 count was 157,031 residents, and a five-member board of supervisors serves four-year terms.

The county grew from a mostly farm economy into a suburban one over the twentieth century, and the population went from almost 44,000 in 1970 to more than 69,000 a decade later. That growth explains the mix a seller meets today: newer subdivisions close to Jackson, older houses in the small towns and rural lots on the edges.

Offices that handle taxes and land records

Three offices matter when you sell: the Tax Assessor, the Tax Collector and the Chancery Clerk. Payments go to the Tax Collector. The other two are below.

OfficeWhat it doesLocation and contact
Tax AssessorValues property and takes homestead applicationsCourthouse Annex, 211 E Government St, Brandon; (601) 825-1470
Chancery ClerkLand records, recording and tax sale redemptionCourthouse Annex Suite D, 211 E Government St; mail to P O Box 700, Brandon 39043; (601) 825-1469; Mon to Fri 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Expect to phone all three offices. The Tax Collector tells you what is owed this year, the Tax Assessor tells you whether homestead is on file and how the parcel is valued, and the Chancery Clerk tells you who holds title and whether the land has any sale or redemption history. Writing down each answer with the date of the call gives your title company something solid to work from.

The clerk's office runs separate pages for e-recording, recording requirements and delinquent taxes. Under state law the clerk is the custodian of land records and also runs the annual county tax sale, as the Department of Revenue explains.

Homestead exemption

File with the Rankin County Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1. The first filing has to be made in person, and the county's Filings and Exemptions page explains that the benefit then renews each year unless your filing status changes.

A fresh application is required after any of these:

  • Marriage, divorce, separation, or the death of a spouse or joint owner.
  • A change in ownership, use or occupancy.
  • Acquiring new property or a change in the property description.
  • Turning sixty-five or becoming 100% disabled for the first time.

The county warns that failing to report a homestead change can mean a fine of up to $5,000, two years in prison, or both. An owner who is 65 or older, or 100% disabled, is generally exempt on 160 acres or about $75,000 of appraised value, whichever limit comes first, and the rest is taxed.

Selling counts as a change in ownership, so tell the Tax Assessor once the deed is recorded. Doing it promptly keeps the exemption record clean and protects you from the fine described above.

How taxes are figured and what happens if they are late

Bills follow the state formula: true value, times the assessment ratio, times the combined millage for your county, your school district and, inside a city, that city. Classification works like this: a home occupied by its owner is rated at 10% of true value and everything else at 15%, as the Department of Revenue FAQ lays out.

The due date is February 1. A parcel left unpaid can go to the county tax auction. Depending on the county, that sale is the first Monday of April or the last Monday of August, and Rankin's own page is where to confirm which.

Once a sale has happened, the Chancery Clerk's Land Redemption page has an online search for delinquent tax amounts and redemption details. Credit card payments carry a 2.5% convenience charge, and debit transactions a $2.25 flat fee. Call the clerk at 601-825-1469 with questions.

A seller who is behind should find the exact amount before listing instead of waiting. Closing stalls until that figure is known, and having it lets you choose between paying now and letting the sale absorb it.

Recording a deed in Rankin County

Because Rankin collects the $1 archive fee, recording a deed of up to five pages costs $26, with $1 added for every page beyond that. That is the statewide schedule under Miss. Code 25-7-9, in effect since January 1, 2020, and the Harrison County Chancery Clerk posts it from the Mississippi Chancery Clerk's Association.

The recorder can add $10 when a document does not follow the format rules in Miss. Code 89-5-24. Fees can change, which is why a short call to the Rankin Chancery Clerk beats guessing at a check amount. Our Mississippi quitclaim deed guide covers format and recording rules in more detail.

What sellers in Rankin County usually face

Three situations account for most Rankin sales that need a little extra care: back taxes, an inherited house, and a place with repairs a buyer's lender would object to. Pulling records together early helps in all three.

  • Get the current tax statement from the Tax Collector and check with the Tax Assessor that homestead is on file.
  • Ask the Chancery Clerk to confirm the deed of record and any tax sale or redemption history.
  • If the house is inherited, learn whether an estate is open and read our probate guide.
  • Watch the county website for posted notices before you plan yard clearing or burning.

A typical sale runs in order: confirm who owns the house and what is owed, sign a contract, let the title company search and clear the title, then close and record the deed with the Chancery Clerk. Anything owed to the county is paid out of your proceeds at the closing table.

Before the first call, put your papers in one place. Bring your deed, your newest tax statement and any mortgage payoff letter, plus the lease if the house is rented. If the house passed through an estate, add the court papers. Having these in one folder lets a title company or a buyer answer ownership questions in a single call instead of several.

Calendar dates deserve a look too. Homestead filings close April 1, the bill is due February 1, and the auction lands in April or August. A sale scheduled to close ahead of the auction date lets the title company pay the county before any buyer can bid, which keeps the tax-deed clock from ever starting.

Pay the Rankin County Tax Collector. The Tax Assessor handles value and homestead exemption, and the Chancery Clerk handles land records and tax sale redemption.

Between January 1 and April 1, in person at the Tax Assessor's office the first time. After that it renews unless something changes, such as ownership, marriage or divorce.

Yes, the county auctions off parcels with unpaid real property tax once a year. State law puts the date on a Monday, either early April or late August, and Rankin's Chancery Clerk posts delinquent tax and redemption details online.

Start informally at the assessor's office, then go formal with the Board of Supervisors if you still disagree. The informal meeting is only a review. Staff pull your property record card, explain how the value was reached, compare your house with similar ones and screen you for exemptions.

A formal appeal starts when you contact the Chancery Clerk at P.O. Box 1240, Oxford, MS 38655 and send a copy to the Tax Collector/Assessor. The county says appeals are stronger when they show comparable properties assessed for less, and it calls a recent appraisal of your own property the best evidence.

At the hearing the board looks at fairness and accuracy. Whether you can afford the bill is not part of the hearing. Foreclosures, short sales, bankruptcy sales, auctions and bank-owned homes are not treated as good sales when true values are set, so a discounted sale next door will not pull your value down.

  • First Monday in July: real and personal property rolls are presented.
  • July: rolls are open to the public.
  • First Monday in August: filing deadline for the Board of Supervisors.
  • Third Monday in August: values and appeals are finalized.

Book your informal review in July while the rolls are open, so you still have time to file formally by the August deadline.

Homestead exemption

Homestead gives the home you live in a lower assessment ratio. Live in your own single-family house and it is assessed at 10 percent of appraised value, not 15. File with the assessor from January 1 to April 1.

Once approved, you stay on the list unless your status changes. Miss April 1 and you lose the exemption for that assessment year. If you are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and otherwise qualify, the first $75,000 of true value is exempt. Eligibility can be lost by not complying with state income tax law or by tagging a car in another county.

Homestead follows the owner, not the house, and that shows up at closing. A buyer who plans to rent the place out may land at the higher ratio. Ask the assessor how a change of ownership is treated before you guess at next year's bill.

How the Lafayette County tax sale works

Oxford-area parcels that stay delinquent go to an online auction at GovEase.com. It starts the last Monday of August and runs 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. daily until every parcel has sold. Bidders register for free and need a Social Security or Tax ID number, a W-9, a way to pay and a maximum bid. The parcels are advertised twice in August in The Oxford Eagle.

By law, overbids go to the county general fund. An owner who redeems pays the original starting amount plus interest. Once two years pass from the purchase date without redemption, the buyer can claim the property by tax deed. Land forfeited to the state can be bought through the Public Lands Division at 601-359-6373, or toll free in Mississippi at 1-866-TFLANDS.

For an owner who is behind, the two-year clock starts at the sale, not when the bill goes late. Close your own sale before the last Monday in August and the title company can pay the taxes at the table.

Common seller situations in Oxford and the county

Four situations come up again and again:

  • Student rentals: a lease may run past the planned closing date, so read it before you set a closing day.
  • Inherited homes: probate runs through the chancery court, and the Chancery Clerk's office is where heirs begin.
  • Delinquent taxes: ask the Tax Collector/Assessor for a payoff figure, and the closing pays it off.
  • Value disputes: the informal review and the August appeal date apply to your parcel whether you plan to sell or stay.

A cash purchase moves faster than a financed one when a property needs work or when the heirs live in different states. Cash Home Buyers evaluates each Lafayette County house individually and does not quote a price or a date before reviewing it.

Recording the deed

The Chancery Clerk records deeds and keeps the land records. The sequence runs from a title search by an attorney or title company, to a deed carrying the seller's notarized signature, a legal description and both parties' details, to recording. Ask the Lafayette clerk whether any local requirement differs.

Since ownership for assessment is fixed as of January 1, spell out in the contract who pays the February 1 bill, and have the title company document that.

How a bill is figured and what late payment costs

The state formula multiplies true value by the assessment ratio and then by the millage rate. The county, a municipality and the school district each set their own levy, and the three add together. A bill still open after February 1 picks up interest of one-half of one percent for each month or part of a month, under Mississippi Code 27-41-9.

Frequently asked questions

When are Lafayette County, MS property taxes due?

They are due February 1. A weekend or legal holiday pushes the penalty-free cutoff to the following Monday.

Does Lafayette County have a separate assessor and collector?

No. One elected Tax Assessor/Collector handles both jobs at 300 N. Lamar Blvd., Suite 103 in Oxford. The assessor line is 662-234-5562 and the collector line is 662-234-6006.

What is the deadline to appeal a Lafayette County assessment?

File with the Board of Supervisors by the first Monday in August. Values are finalized on the third Monday in August, so use July, when the rolls are open, for your informal review.

When is the Lafayette County tax sale?

The online sale at GovEase.com begins on the last Monday of August. After the purchase, the owner gets two years to redeem, and then the buyer can apply for a tax deed.

Can I sell a Lafayette County house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. The title search will list back taxes, and closing pays them out of your proceeds. A house already sold at auction can still be redeemed by the owner within two years.

What is Forrest County, Mississippi, and where does it sit?

Forrest County is a Pine Belt county in southeast Mississippi whose county seat and largest city is Hattiesburg. It was created from Perry County in 1908 and is part of the Hattiesburg metropolitan area. Total area is 470 square miles, nearly all of it land.

Hattiesburg and Petal are the two cities, and a small part of Hattiesburg lies across the line in Lamar County. Smaller places include Glendale, Rawls Springs, Brooklyn, Carnes and McLaurin. Part of De Soto National Forest falls inside the county,. Rural parcels there are valued by the state differently from city lots, since agricultural land is valued by soil type and productivity.

Which roads and neighbors shape a Forrest County sale?

Interstate 59 and U.S. 11, 49 and 98 run through the county, along with Mississippi 13 and 42. Forrest County borders Jones, Perry, Stone, Pearl River, Lamar and Covington counties.

Because Hattiesburg straddles Forrest and Lamar counties, a buyer shopping on the west side of town can end up comparing two tax collectors, two assessors and different millage rates for houses a mile apart. The county line, plus the city of Hattiesburg or Petal levy, decides the bill. Ask the Forrest County Tax Collector which taxing districts apply to your parcel before you quote any monthly cost to a buyer.

Three public school systems operate here, so a Petal address and a Hattiesburg address attend different districts even when the homes look alike. Forrest County Agricultural High School is also in the county.

Who runs property tax in Forrest County?

The county has a Tax Assessor and a Tax Collector, and both offices are at 601 N. Main Street in downtown Hattiesburg. According to the county tax office page, the assessor must locate, classify and assess all taxable property each year, covering roughly 50,000 parcels of real and personal property.

  • Assessor phone: (601) 545-6130, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 1626, Hattiesburg, MS 39403.
  • Collector phone: (601) 582-8228, with statements also handled through P.O. Box 1689, Hattiesburg, MS 39403.
  • The county maps its parcels on TSC Maps, which shows ownership, values, aerial views and legal descriptions.
  • The state requires new aerial photography every ten years, and Forrest County had new photos flown in early 2022.

The Mississippi Department of Revenue adds that assessors must revalue real property at least once every four years. The county tax rolls go to the Board of Supervisors, and the public can review them and file protests before the board and the state approve them.

How is a Forrest County tax bill calculated?

The bill is true value, times the assessment ratio for the property class, times the millage rate set by the taxing bodies. Forrest County's collector applies the ratio and the levy set by the Board of Supervisors and the governing boards of Hattiesburg and Petal.

When are Forrest County taxes due, and what about a deed you just recorded?

Mississippi taxes are due on or before February 1 for the property assessed the previous year, and if that date falls on a weekend or holiday you have until the following Monday. The county site also points out a quirk that affects sellers: the mapping staff work deeds from the previous year, and it can take up to a year for a new owner's name to appear on the land roll.

That lag means a buyer may receive a bill in the seller's name, and a seller may keep receiving statements after closing. Whoever signs the settlement statement should give the Tax Collector a new mailing address, since the office asks taxpayers to report all changes of address or mortgage status. Statements go to mortgage companies or to individuals on the mailing list.

Mobile and manufactured homes follow their own timeline. A mobile home must be registered within seven days of purchase, and the county says taxes are due within 90 days, then each year after. An owner can declare a mobile home as real property for a fee, which changes how it is assessed.

How does homestead exemption work in Forrest County?

Forrest County accepts homestead applications from January 2 to April 1, and the exemption is a one-time filing unless your situation changes. It does not apply to rental property.

The county page says protests are accepted after the rolls are compiled and before the board approves them, without naming a date.

What happens if Forrest County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid real estate taxes put the parcel at risk of a county tax sale. The Department of Revenue says tax sales can be held on the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August, depending on the county.

  • A landowner can redeem within two years after the sale under Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3, as described in Mississippi Supreme Court opinions.
  • Land that finds no buyer goes to the State, and the Secretary of State handles it.
  • Business personal property has a separate rendition due April 1, with a mandatory 10% penalty for missing it.

What should a Forrest County seller expect?

Sellers in Hattiesburg and Petal often deal with timing around closing, a roll that has not caught up with a recent deed, and repairs that a conventional buyer's lender may flag. The Tax Collector is at 601 N. Main Street in downtown Hattiesburg, phone (601) 582-8228. The Tax Assessor is at the same address, phone (601) 545-6130.

Applications are accepted from January 2 to April 1. The county says it is a one-time filing unless something changes, and it does not apply to rental property.

How long does a new deed take to show on the Forrest County roll?

The county says it usually takes up to a year to see your property in your name after you buy, because mapping staff work the previous year's recorded deeds for the current land roll.

Yes. Back taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and a title company will confirm the amount. If the parcel was sold at a tax sale, Mississippi gives the owner two years from the sale to redeem.

Where is Hancock County, Mississippi, and what is in it?

Hancock County sits on the Gulf of Mexico at the Louisiana line, and its county seat is Bay St. Louis. It covers 553 square miles, but 79 of them (14%) are water, which tells you how much of the county is bayou, bay and marsh.

The three cities are Bay St. Louis, Diamondhead and Waveland. Kiln and Pearlington are census-designated places, and smaller communities include Lakeshore, Clermont Harbor, Necaise and Napoleon. The county is part of the Gulfport-Biloxi metropolitan area and is the home of the John C. Stennis Space Center, which Wikipedia describes as NASA's largest rocket engine test facility.

How did Hurricane Katrina change Hancock County housing?

Katrina made its final landfall here on August 29, 2005, and the county's own history is the main reason local sellers talk about storm damage first. Wikipedia's county article reports that not one building or home was left intact along the 7-mile beach front, that nearly the entire first block off the beach was destroyed, and that homes as far as 10 miles inland flooded.

Highway 603 south of Interstate 10 was submerged and the Highway 90 bridge at Bay St. Louis was wrecked. Bay St. Louis, Waveland, Pearlington, Diamondhead and Kiln all took heavy damage. Ask any seller of a coastal house how it fared in 2005, because buyers will.

For a seller this has practical meaning:

  • A buyer's insurer and lender will ask about flood zone and elevation, and a house with past water damage can be hard to finance.
  • With 14% of the county's area covered by water, many parcels sit near the shore, so ask the county or FEMA flood maps where yours falls.
  • A cash buyer who purchases as-is can skip the repair and insurance hurdles that sink conventional contracts, but should still be told about any known damage.

Who assesses and collects property tax in Hancock County?

Hancock County combines the jobs: the County Administrator also serves as Tax Assessor and Collector, according to the Mississippi Association of Supervisors. The Hancock Chamber of Commerce lists the office at 854 Highway 90 in Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 466-5791, and the county's own Tax Assessor page links to tax and fee information and a homestead exemption page.

  • Appeals of an assessment go to the Board of Supervisors, with the Chancery Clerk as the contact.

Call the office before you pay or mail a check.

Real property must be revalued at least every four years, and the assessor does not have to enter your home to do it.

When are Hancock County property taxes due?

The state due date is February 1, and the tax is assessed to whoever owns the parcel on January 1. Bills are issued in November and December, and a February 1 that lands on a weekend or holiday rolls to the following Monday with no penalty or interest.

If taxes stay unpaid, real property can be offered at the county tax sale. After a sale, the owner has two years to redeem under Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3, as summarized in Mississippi Supreme Court opinions. Property nobody buys goes to the State and is handled by the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637.

In practice, sellers should ask for a current payoff and any prior-year balance before they sign a contract. A title company will not close until delinquent taxes are cleared.

How do I contest a Hancock County assessment?

Request a hearing before the Board of Supervisors, using the Chancery Clerk as your point of contact. The Department of Revenue says an appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due, so a homeowner who disagrees with a value cannot wait for the bill in December.

Bring evidence. Storm damage or a wrong square footage on the record are examples of facts worth documenting. The state notes that a refund for prior years can be possible when an appraisal had inaccurate information about home size, and the Chancery Clerk can explain how.

Do homestead exemption and age rules affect a Hancock County sale?

They do, because a buyer who plans to live in the home must apply in their own name. Applications go to the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and the state says you do not reapply each year unless your status changes.

Owners 65 or older, and totally disabled owners who otherwise qualify, are exempt from taxes on the first $75,000 of true value. Eligibility is lost if the owner or spouse is out of compliance with state income tax laws or tags a vehicle in a different county from the home. A seller who has moved out should not keep claiming homestead on a house they no longer occupy.

What do Hancock County sellers usually face?

Sellers here may be dealing with a home that has storm or flood history, an inherited property or a house that has been vacant. Each situation has its own paperwork:

  1. Pull the deed and last tax statement and confirm the current owner on the roll.
  2. Ask the Tax Assessor and Collector for any prior-year balance.
  3. Confirm with the Chancery Clerk that no tax sale is recorded on the parcel.
  4. Gather repair and insurance records so a buyer can price the house honestly.

Who collects property tax in Hancock County?

The Tax Assessor and Collector, a combined office headed by the County Administrator. The Hancock Chamber of Commerce lists it at 854 Highway 90, Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 466-5791. Call to confirm hours and payment methods.

Can I sell a Hancock County house damaged by a storm?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a damaged house as-is. You still need clear title and any taxes paid or settled at closing, and you should disclose damage you know about.

Two years from the date of the tax sale, according to Mississippi Supreme Court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. The Chancery Clerk handles redemption notices and payments.
